result.summary: Pausanias describes the Alcathous citadel at Megara, its monuments, a harp-sounding stone that reminds him of the Memnon Colossus in Egypt, and several temples and statues. He also tells how Alcathous killed his son Callipolis, and records the Megarian cult of Ino.

scenes.title: Citadel of Alcathous and the harp stone
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the monument of Megareus, the altar of the Prodromi and the stone where Apollo laid his harp while helping Alcathous build the wall.

scenes.title: The Colossus at Thebes
scenes.summary: Pausanias compares the stone to the singing statue at Egyptian Thebes, called Memnon, which Cambyses cut in two.

scenes.title: Temples and statues of Megara
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the council chamber, the temples of Athene and Apollo, the ebony statues and the temple of Demeter.

scenes.title: Death of Callipolis
scenes.summary: Callipolis hears of Ischepolis' death, runs to the altar and throws down the wood. Alcathous, not knowing the news, kills him with a piece of it.
scenes.stakes: Callipolis risks his father's anger at his apparent irreverence; he is killed.

scenes.title: Shrine of Ino
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the hero-chapel of Ino and the Megarian story that her body washed ashore and was buried.

alias_notes.explanation: Megarians say Ino was first called Leucothea by them.
Epithet of Athene, linked by Pausanias to Aias.

notable_quotes.reason: The stone that sounds like a harp when struck with a pebble.

analysis.text: Pausanias ties monuments to local legend, showing how places keep memory of heroes and gods.
The comparison with the Memnon Colossus and the mention of Hadrian show Pausanias' Roman-era viewpoint and his travels.

fun_facts.text: The Egyptian statue Pausanias mentions is one of the Colossi of Memnon, which was said to sing at dawn.

language_notes.text: Prodromi means 'runners-before' or forerunners; the gods are so named as advance helpers, here honored at the start of the building.
Refers to the tribute of youths and maidens sent from Athens to Minos of Crete, to be given to the Minotaur; Theseus went with them.
Syringes means 'pipes' or flutes; it names the rock-cut tombs at Thebes, whose narrow passages resembled pipes.
Cambyses, Persian king, conquered Egypt in 525 BC; the statue's breaking and its morning sound were famous.
Decataphorus probably means 'receiver of tithes'; Archegetes means 'founder-leader', a title for Apollo as guide of colonies.
'The wood from the altar' means the sacrificial firewood; throwing it down disrupted the rite, so Alcathous read it as sacrilege.

context_notes.text: Timalcus was a Megarian killed by Theseus, according to Pausanias' earlier account in this book.
Adrian is the Roman emperor Hadrian, who sponsored many building works in Greece in the 2nd century AD.
The Calydonian boar hunt was a heroic expedition led by Meleager, gathering many Greek heroes to kill a monstrous boar.
Ino became the sea goddess Leucothea after leaping into the sea; she was worshipped as a protector of sailors.

literary_notes.text: The statue's morning sound is compared to a harp or lyre with a broken string, giving the reader a concrete image of the sound.
Pausanias openly offers his own conjecture against local guides, showing his critical, personal manner as a traveller-author.
Alcathous kills his son for impiety before learning that the son was only bringing news of his brother's death, making the act tragic.
